'''''Nama hispida''''' is an [[annual plant|annual]] [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Namaceae]].<ref name="WFO">{{Cite WFO |genus=Nama |species=hispida |authority=Boiss. |id=0001066608 |access-date=2026-03-10 }}</ref> Common names include '''sand bells''', '''rough nama''', and '''bristly nama'''. It is native to the American [[Southwestern United States|desert southwest]] and throughout northern and central [[Mexico]].<ref name="SEINet" />

==Description==
''Nama hispida'' is an [[Annual plant|annual]] herb growing 5-30 centimeters tall. The stems are erect to ascending and may further spread with age. The leaves are alternate, slightly broader at the tip and can be 1-7 centimeters long. The leaf bases narrow into a winged [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]], but the upper leaves are smaller and [[Sessility (botany)|sessile]]. All the foliage is [[Pubescence (botany)|pubescent]].<ref name=SEINet/>

The [[flower]]s are bright purple, lavender, or pink, and arranged in small clusters at branch tips or they are solitary in [[leaf axil]]s. The [[Sepal|calyces]] have 5 lobes and are divided nearly to the base. The [[Corolla (botany)|corolla]] has a funnel to bell shape, 5 lobes, and is roughly 8-15 millimeters long and nearly as wide at the top. The [[fruit]] is a [[Capsule (fruit)|capsule]] with many tiny [[seed]]s.<ref name=SEINet>[https://swbiodiversity.org/seinet/taxa/index.php?taxauthid=1&taxon=2035&clid=2751 SEINet Arizona-New Mexico chapter - Nama hispida. Retrieved 2026-01-05.]</ref>

==Distribution==
''Nama hispida'' occurs in the southwestern United States and northern and central Mexico, largely throughout the [[Chihuahuan Desert]]. Its range extends from [[California]] east to [[Oklahoma]] and [[Texas]]. The distribution continues south into [[Baja California|Baja]] and mainland Mexico, until the state of [[Veracruz]]. <ref name=WFO/>

==Ecology==

''Nama hispida'' is frequently, though not exclusively found on gypsum soils.<ref name="Dissertation">{{cite thesis |last=Taylor |first=Sarah |date=2012 |title=Molecular Systematics and the Origins of Gypsophily in Nama L. (Boraginaceae) |url=https://repositories.lib.utexas.edu/items/574fb051-55ce-4d98-a22c-1a3b30802b18 |work= |degree=PhD |location=Austin, Texas |publisher= The University of Texas at Austin|url-status=live |archive-url=http://hdl.handle.net/2152/ETD-UT-2012-05-5752 |archive-date=2012-07-17 |access-date=2026-04-01}}</ref>

[[Halictidae|Halictid]] bees of the genera [[Sphecodosoma]] and [[Conanthalictus]] have been reported as frequent pollinators of ''N.hispida''.<ref name="Tyrl">{{cite journal |last1=Tyrl |first1=Ronald J. |last2=Erteeb |first2=Fathi B. |last3=Bruner |first3=Joe L. |last4=Ezell |first4=Wayland L. |last5=Estes |first5=James R. |last6=Grummer |first6=Bruce |title=A Biosystematic Study of the Relationship of Nama hispidum and Nama stevensii (Hydrophyllaceae) |journal=The Southwestern Naturalist |date=1984 |volume=29 |issue=4 |pages=367–375 |doi=10.2307/3670988 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3670988?seq=8 |access-date=2026-04-01 |issn=0038-4909 |url-status=live|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Uses==
''Nama hispida'' has been used by the [[Navajo]] to treat spider bites.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Moerman |first1=Daniel E. |title=Native American medicinal plants : an ethnobotanical dictionary |date=2009 |publisher=Portland, Or. : Timber Press |isbn=978-1-60469-035-4 |url=https://archive.org/details/nativeamericanme0000moer/page/8/mode/2up |access-date=5 April 2026}}</ref>
